title: BEFORE SAMSON WAS BORN, GOD GAVE HIS MOTHER A WARNING THAT WOULD CHANGE EVERYTHING
paragraphs: BEFORE SAMSON WAS BORN, GOD GAVE HIS MOTHER A WARNING THAT WOULD CHANGE EVERYTHING

She was barren. Her nation was broken. Her child had not even taken his first breath. Yet heaven was already speaking about his destiny. What God told this unnamed mother reveals something terrifying about wasted calling—and something beautiful about the grace that can still reach us after everything falls apart.

There is something heartbreaking about realizing that a person can be chosen by God, gifted beyond imagination, surrounded by divine opportunities… and still make decisions that destroy what they were meant to protect.
But there is something even more astonishing.
God can begin writing a story of deliverance long before the person involved understands what is at stake.
And sometimes, the first person entrusted with that story isn't a king, a prophet, or a warrior.
Sometimes it's a woman whose name Scripture never even tells us.
A woman who has spent years living with an unanswered prayer.
A woman who has watched other mothers hold their children while her own arms remained empty.
A woman who probably never imagined that heaven would interrupt her ordinary life with instructions about a child she had not yet conceived.
And what God told her was extraordinary.
She was not to drink wine.
She was not to drink strong drink.
She was not to eat anything unclean.
Not because God was condemning every mother who had ever eaten differently.
Not because wine itself was universally forbidden to every Israelite.
But because the child she would carry had been set apart for a particular divine calling before his birth.
And the tragedy?
That child would eventually become one of the strongest men in the Bible.
Yet his greatest battles would not be against the Philistines.
They would be against the desires he repeatedly refused to master.
His name was Samson.
But before we talk about his strength, his failures, the woman who betrayed him, or the prison where his eyes were taken from him, we need to return to the woman who first heard the promise.
Because the story begins not with a powerful man…
But with a mother receiving a word from God.
“And the angel of the LORD appeared unto the woman, and said unto her, Behold now, thou art barren, and bearest not: but thou shalt conceive, and bear a son.” — Judges 13:3 (KJV)
Read that again.
God did not begin by describing her future son's muscles.
He began by acknowledging her present pain.
You are barren.
Heaven knew.
The years of waiting had not escaped God's attention.
The disappointment had not made her invisible.
Her inability to conceive was not proof that she had been forgotten.
And then came the promise.
You shall conceive and bear a son.
Can you imagine that moment?
No pregnancy test.
No medical confirmation.
No visible evidence that anything had changed.
Only a divine announcement spoken into a life where the impossible had become painfully familiar.
And immediately, the messenger gave her instructions.
“Now therefore beware, I pray thee, and drink not wine nor strong drink, and eat not any unclean thing.” — Judges 13:4 (KJV)
Then came the explanation.

“For, lo, thou shalt conceive, and bear a son; and no razor shall come on his head: for the child shall be a Nazarite unto God from the womb: and he shall begin to deliver Israel out of the hand of the Philistines.” — Judges 13:5 (KJV)
Here is where the story becomes much deeper than a simple warning about what a pregnant woman should consume.
The Hebrew text describes the child as a נְזִיר אֱלֹהִים — nezir Elohim.
A person consecrated, or set apart, to God.
The Hebrew word נָזִיר (nazir) is connected with separation or consecration.
This is the biblical background of the Nazirite commitment described in Numbers 6.
Ordinarily, a Nazirite vow involved abstaining from products of the grapevine, avoiding contact with the dead, and allowing the hair to remain uncut during the period of consecration.
But Samson's calling was unusual.
It was announced before his conception.
And according to Judges 13:7, his consecration was to extend from the womb until the day of his death.
His mother's instructions concerning wine, strong drink, and unclean food belonged to this particular sacred calling.
The Hebrew expression כָּל־טָמֵא (kol-tame) means anything unclean in the relevant ritual sense.
This was not a modern dietary program or a universal command that every pregnant woman must adopt the Nazirite restrictions.
It was an instruction given in a specific covenantal setting, connected to a child appointed for a specific mission.
And there is another detail we must not miss.
The angel did not say Samson would completely deliver Israel.
He said Samson would begin to deliver Israel from the Philistines.
That single word matters.
Samson was never meant to be the ultimate Savior.
He was a flawed instrument in a much larger story of God's faithfulness.
And that is where the warning reaches us.
Because some of us have confused being gifted with being spiritually mature.
We think that because God has used us, our private compromises must not matter.
We think that because people admire our strength, our hidden weaknesses are harmless.
We think that because our ministry is growing, our hearts must be healthy.
But Samson's life confronts that illusion.
A divine calling does not make a person immune to the consequences of disobedience.
And spiritual gifts are never permission to abandon spiritual faithfulness.
Before Samson was born, his mother was instructed to treat his calling seriously.
Yet when Samson grew up, the story repeatedly shows him treating holy things carelessly.
He pursued relationships that brought him into conflict with his parents and exposed him to serious danger.
He approached the carcass of a lion and took honey from it, an episode that raises troubling questions about his Nazirite consecration.
He repeatedly allowed desire, anger, pride, and revenge to shape his decisions.
And eventually, he entered a relationship with Delilah that became the setting for his downfall.
The woman who had carried him was careful about what entered her body.
The son she carried would struggle with what he allowed to rule his heart.
That contrast should make us uncomfortable.
Not because Samson's mother was responsible for his adult decisions.
She was not.
Parents cannot guarantee the faithfulness of their children by perfectly obeying God themselves.
And children are not condemned to repeat the failures of their parents.
But the contrast reveals a painful truth.
You can inherit a remarkable opportunity without choosing to honor it.
You can be raised around Scripture and still resist the God of Scripture.
You can grow up hearing prayers and still develop a secret life that contradicts everything you profess.
You can know the language of holiness while privately negotiating with temptation.
And perhaps the most frightening part of Samson's story is that his downfall did not happen all at once.
It unfolded through repeated decisions.
One compromise.
One rationalization.
One moment of confidence that he could get closer to danger without being overcome by it.
Until the day came when he woke up expecting the strength he had known before.
But something had changed.
“And he wist not that the LORD was departed from him.” — Judges 16:20 (KJV)
Those words are devastating.
He did not know.
He assumed the next escape would look like the previous escapes.
He assumed that because he had survived earlier compromises, he could survive another.
But the Lord had departed from him in the sense that the divine empowerment he had relied upon was no longer present.
His enemies seized him.
They put out his eyes.
They brought him down to Gaza.
They bound him with bronze shackles.
And the man who had once terrified the Philistines was forced to grind grain in prison.
Imagine that darkness.
The sound of chains.
The humiliation.
The memory of every warning he had ignored.
The realization that the people who once feared him were now celebrating his defeat.
He had been called to confront the Philistines.
Now he was their prisoner.
He had been given extraordinary strength.
Now he could not even defend himself.
He had spent so much of his life following what pleased his eyes.
Now his eyes were gone.
And somewhere in the background of that tragedy stands the memory of a mother who had received a promise before he was born.
We do not know whether she was still alive when Samson fell.
Scripture does not tell us.
We should not invent her presence at his prison or claim to know what she felt.
But we do know that God had spoken to her about this child's purpose.
And we know that Samson's life became a terrible warning about what happens when calling and character move in opposite directions.
Perhaps that is why this story feels so personal.
Because most of us will never tear apart a lion.
We will never carry the gates of a city on our shoulders.
We will never defeat a thousand enemies with the jawbone of a donkey.
But we know what it means to keep returning to something that is destroying us.
We know what it means to promise God that this will be the last time.
The last lie.
The last secret conversation.
The last night of feeding an addiction.
The last compromise that nobody else knows about.
The last moment of pretending everything is fine while something inside us is quietly collapsing.
And we know how easy it is to confuse the absence of immediate consequences with God's approval.
But delayed consequences are not divine permission.
And God's patience must never be mistaken for indifference.
Still, the story does not end with Samson's humiliation.
There is a verse in Judges 16 that almost whispers hope into the darkness.
“Howbeit the hair of his head began to grow again after he was shaven.” — Judges 16:22 (KJV)
His hair began to grow again.
That detail is powerful.
But we must understand it correctly.
Samson's hair was not a magical source of supernatural energy.
His strength came from the Lord.
The uncut hair was an outward sign of his consecration.
Its regrowth was not an automatic guarantee that spiritual power had returned.
Yet the narrator places that detail in the story before Samson's final prayer.
And the reader is invited to keep watching.
Because the man who had repeatedly relied on his strength was about to cry out in his weakness.
“And Samson called unto the LORD, and said, O Lord GOD, remember me, I pray thee, and strengthen me, I pray thee, only this once, O God…” — Judges 16:28 (KJV)
Remember me.
What a prayer.
Not a speech about his accomplishments.
Not a reminder of how many Philistines he had defeated.
Not an argument that he deserved another chance.
A desperate appeal to the God who had empowered him.
Samson's prayer was also mixed with a desire for vengeance over his eyes. Scripture does not present every motive or action of Samson as an example for believers to imitate.
His final act brought down the Philistine temple, killing himself and many Philistines.
It was a violent conclusion in the historical context of Israel's oppression, not a model for Christian revenge or self-destruction.
Yet Hebrews 11:32 later names Samson among figures remembered in the history of faith.
That does not erase his sins.
It reminds us that God's work through deeply imperfect people cannot be reduced to either their greatest victories or their worst failures.
And here is where we must look beyond Samson.
Because if we stop with a tragic hero whose hair grew back, we will miss the greater hope toward which Scripture points.
Samson was announced before his birth.
So was Jesus.
Samson's birth brought hope to an oppressed people.
Jesus came as the promised Savior of His people.
Samson was set apart for a mission he would fulfill imperfectly.
Jesus was holy and fulfilled the Father's will without sin.
Samson's life exposed the weakness of even the strongest human deliverer.
Jesus revealed the power of God through perfect obedience, sacrificial love, His death, and His resurrection.
Samson began a deliverance that was limited and incomplete.
Jesus accomplished the decisive work of redemption from sin and death.
And the contrast is breathtaking.
Samson was strong, but could be overcome by his own desires.
Jesus was tempted, yet without sin.
Samson was betrayed and captured after repeated personal compromises.
Jesus was betrayed and arrested, though He had committed no sin.
Samson died bringing judgment upon his enemies.
Jesus willingly laid down His life for sinners, even praying for those who crucified Him.
And unlike Samson, Jesus did not remain dead.
He rose again.
This is why Christianity cannot be reduced to a message about becoming a stronger version of yourself.
If the Gospel were merely about trying harder, Samson's story would leave us with nothing but fear.
Be more disciplined.
Avoid temptation.
Protect your calling.
Never fail.
Those warnings have their place.
But warnings alone cannot save a guilty soul.
We need more than a stronger will.
We need a Savior.
We need forgiveness for the sins we have already committed.
We need a new heart.
We need grace that does not excuse our rebellion but brings us to repentance and transforms the direction of our lives.
And that is what Jesus Christ offers.
The Greek New Testament uses the word χάρις (charis) for grace.
In Ephesians 2:8–9, salvation is described as God's gift, received through faith, not something we earn through our works.
And Ephesians 2:10 continues by teaching that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace is not permission to remain enslaved to sin.
Grace is God's undeserved favor that saves us and leads us into a new life.
You do not earn salvation by becoming holy enough for Jesus to accept you. You come to Jesus because you cannot save yourself, and His grace begins changing you.
That distinction changes everything.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying a private failure.
Maybe you have spent years appearing spiritually strong while silently losing battles nobody knows you are fighting.
Maybe you are a parent praying for a son or daughter who has wandered far from God.
Maybe you are the child who grew up in a praying home and now feels ashamed of how far you have gone.
Or maybe you are the person who has been told so many times that you have ruined your life that you have started believing your story cannot be redeemed.
Listen carefully.
Samson's story does not promise that every consequence will disappear.
It does not promise that lost opportunities will always return.
It does not promise that every broken relationship will be restored exactly as it was.
But the Gospel declares something greater than the restoration of earthly circumstances.
In Jesus Christ, your sin does not have to be the final word over your eternity.
The apostle John wrote:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9 (KJV)
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
The invitation is not to conceal sin behind religious activity.
It is to bring it into the light before the Lord.
To repent.
To trust Christ.
To stop treating His mercy as an excuse for disobedience and begin receiving it as the foundation of a transformed life.
And for the mother who is still praying, there is another truth worth holding close.
Samson's mother was faithful to receive God's instructions.
Yet Samson still made destructive choices.
Your child's rebellion is not automatic proof that you failed as a parent.
You are responsible for your own obedience, but you are not the Holy Spirit.
You cannot repent on behalf of another person.
You cannot force someone to love Christ.
You can teach.
You can pray.
You can model repentance and faith.
You can speak truth with love.
But the work of changing a heart belongs to God.
Do not turn Samson's story into a weapon against mothers whose children have wandered.
Let it instead remind us that even children raised with extraordinary spiritual opportunities must personally respond to God.
And do not turn the instructions about wine and unclean food into a promise that following a special diet will guarantee a godly child.
That is not what Judges 13 teaches.
The central issue is God's initiative, His holy calling, and the seriousness of responding faithfully to His word.
This mother was asked to obey before she could see the promise fulfilled.
And that is a challenge for every generation.
Will we obey God when obedience is inconvenient?
Will we trust Him when our circumstances seem unchanged?
Will we take His Word seriously when the culture around us calls holiness outdated?
Will we teach our children that being set apart for God is not about looking superior to others, but about belonging to Him?
Will we remember that the goal of Christian parenting is not to raise impressive children who bring honor to our family name, but to point them toward the Lord Jesus Christ?
And if we are the ones who have wandered, will we stop running?
Because the most urgent question is not whether you have Samson's strength.
It is whether you have surrendered to Samson's greater Savior.
The world admires strength.
Jesus calls us to acknowledge our need for Him.
The world celebrates independence.
Jesus calls us to abide in Him.
The world tells us to hide our failures until we can rebuild our image.
Jesus calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness through His blood.
Perhaps you have been trying to prove that you are still strong.
Still capable.
Still respectable.
Still worthy of admiration.
But the prayer you need tonight may be much simpler.
Lord Jesus, I have sinned. I cannot rescue myself. Have mercy on me. Forgive me. Teach me to walk in Your truth. Change what I have kept hidden. I surrender my life to You.
There is no magic in repeating those words.
The power is not in a formula.
Salvation is found in Jesus Christ, who died for our sins and rose again, and who calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
And if this message has uncovered something in your heart, do not rush past that moment.
Be honest before God.
You do not need to expose intimate details or make a public confession to earn God's forgiveness. He already knows your heart.
But your honest words may encourage another person who thought they were the only one struggling.
And perhaps there is someone on your Facebook friends list who needs this message tonight.
A mother who has almost given up praying.
A father carrying quiet regret.
A young believer fighting temptation.
A person who still attends church but feels spiritually empty.
Or someone who has never understood why Jesus came to save sinners.
There is also something I want to share with those who believe this work of proclaiming the Gospel should continue reaching more people.
Gospel Warrior is more than a place to read an occasional article.
We want it to be a place where people who are struggling, questioning, repenting, healing, and growing in faith can keep finding biblical nourishment.
Our desire is to keep these resources available, to continue producing Christ-centered content, and to expand the reach of this ministry so that more people can encounter the truth of Scripture.
And that kind of work requires people who are willing to stand alongside it.
For those who choose to make it part of their regular Christian giving, it can be an expression of generosity offered to God in gratitude, much like other voluntary ministry offerings.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
We never want anyone to feel that they must purchase something to glorify God.
These items are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
You are welcome here.
Keep reading.
Keep praying.
Keep growing in the Word.
We do not know every person who will read these words.
We do not know whose heart may be softened.
We do not know who may finally open a Bible, confess a hidden sin, seek reconciliation, or begin asking serious questions about Jesus.
But we know the Gospel is worth proclaiming.
Our responsibility is to be faithful with the message.
The results belong to God.
Now, before you leave, return with me one last time to that unnamed mother in Judges 13.
She had no idea how complicated her son's life would become.
She did not know the details of the battles he would fight.
She did not know the terrible decisions he would make.
She did not know that future generations would still be reading his story thousands of years later.
She only knew that God had spoken.
And that she was being called to respond.
Perhaps that is where you are today.
You cannot see the whole story.
You do not know what tomorrow will bring.
You do not know whether the person you are praying for will finally turn back to God.
You do not know how the Lord may use your quiet faithfulness.
But you can obey the truth He has already revealed.
You can turn away from sin.
You can trust Jesus Christ.
You can pray for your children without trying to control their souls.
You can tell someone what Christ has done for you.
And you can remember that the strongest person in the room is not necessarily the one with the greatest spiritual maturity.
Sometimes the person who most clearly understands grace is the one who has finally stopped pretending to be strong enough without Jesus.
Samson's life began with a divine announcement.
His story ended in tragedy, judgment, and a final act through which God worked against Israel's oppressors.
But the story of Jesus does not end in a tomb.
The stone was rolled away.
The crucified Savior rose.
And because He lives, those who repent and believe in Him have a hope that does not depend on human strength, perfect parenting, an unblemished past, or the approval of the world.
So if you remember only one thing from this story, remember this:
God did not send His Son merely to help strong people become stronger. He sent His Son to save sinners who could never save themselves.
And that includes people with complicated stories.
People with hidden wounds.
People who have fallen.
People who are ashamed.
People who are ready to stop running.
People like us.
What is one area of your life where you need to stop relying on your own strength and begin surrendering more fully to Jesus?
You can answer in a sentence, a testimony, or simply write “Lord, teach me to surrender.”
And if you know someone who needs to hear that their failures do not place them beyond the reach of Christ's mercy, send this to them today.
Because the most unforgettable part of Samson's story is not that his hair began to grow again.
It is that his life reminds us how desperately we need a Deliverer who will never fail.
Samson could not save himself from the ruins of his own choices—but Jesus Christ entered the ruins of our sin to accomplish the salvation we could never achieve.
